name: Measuring and Improving Reasoning in Humans and Machines
summary: How human and AI reasoning goes wrong, how to measure and improve it, and how to design tests and human–AI interactions that reward better reasoning.
desc: The mechanisms that produce belief in us have largely been shaped by pressures that are not aimed at truth: natural selection, social approval, and institutional incentives. Language models are shaped by their own imperfect optimization pressures, including next-token prediction and feedback from human evaluators. This interdisciplinary seminar asks how those pressures affect reasoning in humans and machines, and what we can do to improve it.
details: We consider how to characterize cognitive errors, which interventions improve reasoning, and whether improvements transfer across tasks. A recurring question concerns measurement: can we devise tests of good reasoning where improving a score requires improving the underlying skill? We also examine sycophancy, confabulation, and deception in language models, and ask how reflection, training, and collaboration might produce more reliable epistemics.

The course brings philosophical analysis into conversation with empirical work in psychology and AI. Student projects move from concepts such as intellectual humility or probabilistic calibration to proposals for measurement and systematic improvement. Graduate students from other disciplines are welcome.

name: Philosophy of Emerging Technology
summary: How to shape a better future in a world of AI, human enhancement, climate technology, and engineered viruses: well-being, agency, and risks.
desc: This course explores philosophical issues raised by recent and near-future technologies, including artificial intelligence, climate engineering, virtual reality, surveillance, gene editing, treatments for aging, and engineered viruses. We consider how these technologies may affect human well-being and agency, evaluate their risks, and ask how we might help shape a better future.
details: The course asks how AI may change work, relationships, and our access to knowledge; what principles should guide artificial agents; and what would make an artificial mind conscious or deserving of moral consideration. We also examine surveillance and autonomy, biosecurity, climate engineering, interventions in wild and farmed animals, and the ethics of human enhancement.

Questions of governance and responsibility run throughout: which technologies should we develop, who should control them, and how should we weigh immediate benefits against catastrophic risks and effects on future generations?

name: Global Priorities
summary: An interdisciplinary course on the world’s most important problems and how to help: global health and poverty, animals and the environment, and emerging technologies.
desc: What would we do if we cared about everyone equally? This course investigates the world’s most important problems and what we can do to help with our careers, time, and resources. We focus on global health and poverty, animals and the environment, and emerging technologies, asking how to compare problems, assess evidence, and choose among interventions when resources are limited.
details: The course draws on development economics, global health, environmental science, international studies, and progress studies. We examine both particular interventions and the institutions that make progress possible: research funding, incentives, coordination, regulation, and the capacity to implement policy. Topics include health and development, climate and energy, animal welfare, AI, demographic change, and global catastrophic risk.

Philosophical questions include how to weigh health, freedom, opportunity, and happiness; how much future people and nonhuman animals matter; and what responsibilities individuals have to improve the world. PHIL 360 is a more advanced version of PHIL 250: Changing the World, with substantial overlap and more demanding engagement with arguments and evidence.

name: Critical Reasoning
summary: Practical reasoning tools from philosophy, cognitive psychology, and behavioral economics: logic, probability, decision theory, biases, evidence, and causation.
desc: Reason better when deciding what to believe and when deciding what to do. This course provides practical tools drawn from cognitive psychology, behavioral economics, logic, probability, and decision theory. We examine heuristics and biases—spontaneous judgments that can be predictably irrational—and study what good deductive, causal, and probabilistic reasoning looks like.
details: The goal is to develop effective reasoning skills with applications in personal and professional life: recognizing and constructing compelling arguments, assessing evidence, distinguishing correlation from causation, updating beliefs, and making decisions under uncertainty. The course is open to students from across the University.
My textbook, Reason Better: An Interdisciplinary Guide to Critical Thinking, grew out of this course.

name: Philosophy of the Future
summary: Human enhancement and life extension, the value of future populations, and the ethical and philosophical questions raised by artificial general intelligence.
desc: This graduate seminar examines philosophical issues raised by future technology. The prospect of significant human enhancement prompts questions about human nature, personal identity, well-being, and the desirability of vastly extended lifespans. Looking further ahead, we ask how much we should care about distant outcomes and which visions of humanity’s future are worth working toward.
details: How should we weigh equality against autonomy, average well-being against total well-being, and conserving existing forms of life against creating new ones? How should the value of individual subjects—human, posthuman, or animal—relate to the value of species and ecosystems? These questions bear on population ethics and the importance of reducing existential risk.
The possibility of artificial general intelligence also raises questions in ethics and the philosophy of mind, alongside the practical problem of aligning artificial agents with our values.
